newsitem.title: UK: Welsh scientists find the key to greener valleys.
newsitem.headline: Welsh scientists find the key to greener valleys.

text.p: British scientists have found the key to keeping grass green even through the worst drought, the New Scientist magazine reported on Thursday.
It said the discovery could make it cheaper to maintain golf courses, parks and sports pitches, and could also help to produce more nutritious winter feed for farm animals.
The scientists at the Institute of Grassland and Environmental Research noticed a strain of meadow fescue grass which remained green when surrounding grass yellowed because of lack of rain.
They discovered that the grass was a natural mutant which lacks an enzyme that breaks down chlorophyll, the green pigment plants use to make their own food through photosynthesis.

Plant breeders at the institute, at Aberystwyth in central Wales, have now transferred the characteristic to other grasses. "They even retain their greenness in dry conditions when they go crispy," one researcher, Howard Thomas, told the magazine.

Thomas said the discovery could bring a bonus to farmers, since chlorophyll is bound chemically to compounds called "light-harvesting proteins" which account for up to 30 percent of the protein in grass.

Normally these proteins are lost when farmers make silage to feed their animals during the winter, being broken down into peptides and amino acids. But this would not happen in grasses lacking the crucial enzyme.
Wales is already known for its verdant pastures thanks to the Richard Llewellyn novel How Green was My Valley and the Tom Jones song The Green, Green Grass of Home.
